modules.title: Hand Rankings & Board Textures
modules.description: Understand the official hierarchy of poker hands and how board cards change hand strength.

lessons.title: The Royal Flush & Straight Flushes
lessons.coreConcept: A Royal Flush is the mathematically unbeatable peak of Texas Hold'em (Ace through Ten of the same suit).
lessons.content:
Welcome to the absolute pinnacle of poker: The Royal Flush.

This is the highest possible hand in Texas Hold'em, and hitting it is incredibly rare. Statistically, you have a 1 in 30,939 chance of flopping a Royal Flush when holding two suited Broadway cards, and an overall 1 in 649,739 chance of making it by the river.

It consists of an Ace, King, Queen, Jack, and 10 of the exact same suit. Because it is the highest straight flush possible, it is mathematically unbeatable. When you hold a Royal Flush, your only objective is extracting maximum chips without scaring your opponents into folding.

Just below it sits the Straight Flush: any five consecutive cards of identical suit (e.g., 5-6-7-8-9 of clubs). If two players both make a straight flush, the player with the higher top card takes the pot.
lessons.proTip: Never slow-play a Royal Flush to the point of checking the river. Make a reasonable value bet to give opponents holding flushes or full houses an excuse to pay you off.
lessons.commonMistake: Panicking and shoving all-in instantly when hitting the nuts on the flop, causing everyone else to fold immediately.
lessons.goldenRule: The Royal Flush cannot be beaten—focus 100% of your energy on building the pot.

decisionChallenge.question: You flop a Royal Flush in position on a Qh-Jh-10h flop. The opponent bets $20 into a $40 pot. What is the optimal play?
options: Shove all-in immediately to protect your hand
Call smoothly to keep the opponent's bluffs and lower flushes in the pot
Fold because the board is too wet
decisionChallenge.explanation: Calling smoothly conceals your monster strength and allows your opponent to keep betting their bluffs, straight draws, or smaller flushes on the turn and river.

lessons.title: Quads, Full Houses & The Kicker Problem
lessons.coreConcept: Four of a Kind (Quads) and Full Houses (Boats) win the vast majority of showdowns, but kicker rank breaks ties.
lessons.content:
Four of a Kind (Quads) occurs when you hold all four cards of the same rank (e.g., four Queens). If the board contains four of a kind, the player with the highest fifth card ('kicker') wins.

A Full House consists of three cards of one rank and two of another (e.g., Kings full of 8s: K-K-K-8-8). When two players have a Full House, the higher three-of-a-kind always wins. For example, 9-9-9-2-2 beats 8-8-8-A-A.

The 'Kicker Problem': In Hold'em, every final hand uses exactly 5 cards. When you and your opponent both make one pair (such as a Pair of Aces), the player whose second card is higher wins the entire pot. Holding A-K is vastly more profitable than holding A-4 because your King kicker dominates weaker Aces.
lessons.proTip: Be wary when holding weak Aces like A-2 or A-5. Even when you hit an Ace on the flop, you are frequently 'dominated' by opponents with better kickers.
lessons.commonMistake: Overvaluing a low full house when the board is paired high (e.g., holding 2-2 on a K-K-K-8-2 board—almost any higher pocket pair beats you).
lessons.goldenRule: Kickers decide close pots: play cards with high kickers to avoid being dominated.

visualSpot.handDescription: Pair of Aces with King Kicker beats Pair of Aces with 8 Kicker

lessons.title: Board Textures: Dry vs. Wet Boards
lessons.coreConcept: The flop texture dictates whether top pair is a fortress or a fragile liability.
lessons.content:
Every flop falls somewhere on a spectrum between 'Bone Dry' and 'Soaking Wet'.

A **Dry Board** (e.g., K♠ 7♦ 2♣) features disconnected ranks and mixed suits. There are virtually no flush draws and no open-ended straight draws. On dry boards, Top Pair is strong, and opponents rarely have huge hands. You can bet small to protect your hand and extract value.

A **Wet Board** (e.g., J♥ 10♥ 9♣) features coordinated ranks and multiple cards of the same suit. Straight draws and flush draws are everywhere. Top pair on a wet board is vulnerable, and large bets are necessary to charge drawing hands if you intend to continue.

A **Monotone Board** (e.g., K♠ 8♠ 3♠) has three cards of the exact same suit. Anyone holding a single spade has a flush draw, and players without a spade must proceed with caution.
lessons.proTip: On dry rainbow boards, bet small (25% to 33% pot). On wet connected boards, bet larger (66% to 75% pot) to deny opponents cheap odds to chase draws.
lessons.commonMistake: Slow-playing two pair on a wet board with two flush cards, giving opponents free cards to hit their straights and flushes.
lessons.goldenRule: Wet boards demand defense and larger sizing; dry boards favor small, frequent bets.

modules.title: Table Geography & Positional Power
modules.description: Learn why position is the single greatest competitive edge in Texas Hold'em.

lessons.title: The Button (BTN): The King of the Table
lessons.coreConcept: Acting last on the Flop, Turn, and River gives you complete information before making your move.
lessons.content:
In poker, information is currency. The Button (Dealer position) is universally acknowledged as the most profitable seat at any table.

Why? Because after pre-flop action, the Button acts last on every subsequent street: Flop, Turn, and River. You observe whether your opponents check in weakness, bet small, or show aggression before committing a single chip.

When opponents check to you on the Button, you can take down the pot with a simple bluff. When they bet huge, you can fold without losing chips. This structural informational edge allows you to play the widest, most profitable range of hands in the game (around 40% to 50% of all starting hands).
lessons.proTip: Attack the blinds relentlessly from the Button. If players before you fold, raise with broadways, suited connectors, and pairs to steal the blinds.
lessons.commonMistake: Playing too tight on the Button. Folding hands like K-8s or 9-7s from the Button gives away free money in the long run.
lessons.goldenRule: Position is power: Play more hands in position, fewer hands out of position.

lessons.title: Under the Gun (UTG) & Early Position Discipline
lessons.coreConcept: Acting first with 5 to 8 players behind you requires strict hand selection to avoid traps.
lessons.content:
The seat immediately to the left of the Big Blind is called 'Under the Gun' (UTG). It is named after the feeling of having a pistol pointed at you—because you have zero information about what everyone else holds.

When you open from UTG, there are multiple opponents left to act. The statistical likelihood that at least one of them wakes up with an Ace, King, or high pair is very high. Furthermore, you will be out of position for the entire hand.

Because of this, your UTG opening range must be disciplined and tight (around 12% to 15% of starting hands). Stick to pocket pairs (77+), strong suited broadways (AK, AQ, AJ, KQ suited), and premium offsuit Aces (AKo, AQo).
lessons.proTip: If you are unsure whether to raise a marginal hand like K-10 offsuit from UTG, fold it. Folding marginal hands from early position saves hundreds of big blinds over time.
lessons.commonMistake: Open-limping or raising weak hands like K-J offsuit or A-6 offsuit from UTG, only to face 3-bets from players in position.
lessons.goldenRule: Early position demands discipline: fold marginal cards and build a tight fortress.

lessons.title: The Blinds (SB & BB): Defending the Tax Seats
lessons.coreConcept: You are forced to pay blinds every orbit; defending requires balancing pot odds against positional disadvantage.
lessons.content:
The Small Blind (SB) and Big Blind (BB) are forced bets posted before cards are dealt. Without blinds, players would simply fold until dealt Pocket Aces with zero consequence.

The Blinds are the biggest financial leak for most players. You are forced to invest money with random cards, and you are guaranteed to act first (out of position) on every post-flop street against late-position raisers.

In the Big Blind, you get a 'discount' to call because your 1 BB is already in the pot. If a player opens for 2.2 BB, you only need to call 1.2 BB to see a flop. However, do not defend with trash cards (like 9-3 offsuit) because playing out of position postflop will cost you even more chips.
lessons.proTip: From the Small Blind, prefer 3-betting (re-raising) or folding over calling. Flat-calling from the SB invites the Big Blind to squeeze or see a cheap flop while keeping you out of position.
lessons.commonMistake: Defending every single hand in the Big Blind because 'I already have money in the pot'.
lessons.goldenRule: Blinds are an unavoidable cost—minimize losses with disciplined defense and timely 3-bets.

lessons.title: Quiz: The Positional Advantage
lessons.question: Which position has the greatest strategic advantage across all post-flop betting rounds?

modules.title: The 4 Streets of Combat
modules.description: Learn the chronological anatomy of a Texas Hold'em hand from Pre-Flop to Showdown.

lessons.title: Pre-Flop: The Initial Setup
lessons.coreConcept: Each player receives two private cards; betting establishes who holds initiative going into the flop.
lessons.content:
A hand begins with each player receiving two private 'hole cards'. The player to the left of the Big Blind (UTG) starts the action.

Every player has three fundamental choices:
1. **Fold**: Relinquish cards and forfeit any blinds posted.
2. **Call**: Match the highest bet placed so far (at minimum, 1 Big Blind).
3. **Raise**: Increase the bet, forcing opponents to match the higher amount to continue.

Pre-flop action determines who holds the 'Initiative'. The last aggressive raiser is known as the preflop aggressor and generally has the mathematical right to continue betting on the flop.
lessons.proTip: Never open a pot with a limp (flat calling 1 BB). Always come in with a raise (usually 2.2x to 3x the Big Blind) to seize initiative and thin the field.
lessons.commonMistake: Calling raises with weak offsuit hands from out of position.
lessons.goldenRule: Pre-flop sets the foundation: enter pots with a raise to command the hand.

lessons.title: The Flop: The 71% Commitment Point
lessons.coreConcept: Three community cards are dealt face up. You now know 5 of the 7 cards you will ever see.
lessons.content:
Once pre-flop betting concludes, the dealer burns a card and deals three community cards face up in the middle of the table: The Flop.

The Flop is the most pivotal street in Texas Hold'em. By the flop, you have seen 5 out of 7 total cards (71% of your final holding). You now know whether you hit top pair, flopped a monster set, made a straight draw, or missed entirely.

Action on the flop begins with the first active player seated to the left of the button. If no one has bet yet, players can 'Check' (pass action without investing chips).
lessons.proTip: Check to the pre-flop raiser if you called out of position. Give them the burden of deciding whether to continue betting.
lessons.commonMistake: Donk-betting (leading out with a small bet into the pre-flop raiser), which turns your hand face up and prevents them from bluffing.
lessons.goldenRule: 71% of your hand is known on the flop—evaluate whether your equity justifies further investment.

lessons.title: The Turn: Escalating Stakes
lessons.coreConcept: A fourth card is dealt. Pot sizes swell exponentially, making turn errors costly.
lessons.content:
The dealer burns a card and deals the fourth community card face up: The Turn (also called 'Fourth Street').

Pots on the turn are significantly larger than on the flop. A standard bet on the turn often equals 50% to 75% of the pot, meaning a single call commits a serious portion of your chip stack.

The Turn is where draws mature or miss. If an opponent called your flop bet on a flush draw and a brick turn card falls, their drawing odds drop from ~36% down to ~18%.
lessons.proTip: If you hold a strong value hand, fire a second bet ('double barrel') on the turn to charge opponents holding drawing hands.
lessons.commonMistake: Calling large turn bets with gutshot straight draws (only 4 outs = ~8% equity) when pot odds require 25%+.
lessons.goldenRule: Turn bets are expensive: ensure your hand strength or drawing equity justifies the rising price.

lessons.title: The River & Showdown: Absolute Finality
lessons.coreConcept: The fifth card completes the board. There are no more cards to come—it is pure value or pure bluff.
lessons.content:
The fifth and final community card is revealed: The River ('Fifth Street').

There are no more cards to come. Draws have either made their hand or busted into air. This dynamic changes river strategy completely:
- If you bet, you are either **Value Betting** (hoping a worse hand calls you) or **Bluffing** (hoping a better hand folds).
- Betting a medium-strength hand that only better hands will call is a classic beginner mistake known as 'betting for information'.

If two or more players remain after river betting, the hand goes to Showdown. Players table their hole cards, and the best 5-card combination claims the pot.
lessons.proTip: On the river, ask yourself: 'If I bet, will a worse hand call me?' If the answer is no, check and showdown your hand for free.
lessons.commonMistake: Betting second pair on the river, getting raised, and having to fold when checking would have reached showdown.
lessons.goldenRule: On the river, polarized clarity rules: bet for value or bet as a bluff; check marginal hands.

modules.title: Table Mechanics, Formats & Culture
modules.description: Understand game formats, live vs online play, and psychological discipline.

lessons.title: Cash Games vs. Multi-Table Tournaments (MTTs)
lessons.coreConcept: Cash chips represent real currency with continuous re-buys; tournament chips represent survival.
lessons.content:
Texas Hold'em is played in two distinct formats with completely different strategic rules:

**Cash Games (Ring Games):**
- Chips have direct cash value ($1 chip = $1 cash).
- Blinds remain static forever (e.g., $1/$2 blinds never increase).
- If you lose your chips, you can instantly reach into your wallet and reload to max stack.
- Strategy focuses purely on maximum Expected Value (+EV) per hand without survival fear.

**Tournaments (MTTs & Sit & Gos):**
- Players pay a buy-in to receive a fixed starting chip stack.
- Blinds increase on a countdown timer (e.g., every 10 or 15 minutes).
- When you lose your chips, you are eliminated from the tournament.
- Strategy is governed by the Independent Chip Model (ICM): preserving your tournament life is paramount.
lessons.proTip: Never play tournament hands like cash hands. In tournaments, risk aversion increases near the money bubble because survival guarantees a cash payout.
lessons.commonMistake: Gambling on marginal 50/50 coin-flips early in a tournament when you have a deep stack.
lessons.goldenRule: In cash games, maximize expected value; in tournaments, balance value with tournament survival.

lessons.title: Table Etiquette & The Psychology of Tilt
lessons.coreConcept: Emotional control ('tilt prevention') separates long-term winners from gamblers who blow their bankrolls.
lessons.content:
'Tilt' is a psychological state of emotional frustration, anger, or despair triggered by bad beats or mistakes.

When on tilt, players abandon logic. They start calling large bets with trash, bluffing recklessly into calling stations, and trying to 'win their money back' on the very next hand. Tilt is the #1 reason talented players go broke.

Table Etiquette:
- Always act in turn. Do not fold or declare action before previous players have acted.
- Never reveal your folded cards while a hand is actively contested by other players.
- Respect the clock and avoid slow-rolling (intentionally taking 30 seconds to reveal the winning nuts).
lessons.proTip: Establish a strict 'Stop-Loss' rule: If you lose 3 full buy-ins in a single session, immediately step away from the table for the day.
lessons.commonMistake: Continuing to play while angry after a bad beat, telling yourself 'my luck has to change on the next deal'.
lessons.goldenRule: Master your emotions: a disciplined mind outlasts luck every single time.

modules.title: Poker Math, Pot Odds & Equity Masterclass
modules.description: The exact mathematical framework that professional poker players use to make profitable calls and bets.

lessons.title: The Pot Odds Formula: Risk vs. Reward
lessons.coreConcept: Pot odds tell you the exact percentage of the time your hand must win to break even on a call.
lessons.content:
Welcome to the mathematical engine of poker. Every time an opponent bets and action is on you, you are offered a financial price to call.

The Pot Odds Formula is:
**Pot Odds % = Amount to Call / (Total Pot After You Call)**

Example Scenario:
- The pot has $100.
- Villain bets $50.
- The total pot is now $150, and it costs you $50 to call.
- Total Pot After Call = $100 (original pot) + $50 (villain bet) + $50 (your call) = $200.
- Pot Odds % = $50 / $200 = 0.25 (25%).

This means if your hand has more than 25% Equity (chance of winning), calling is mathematically profitable in the long run. If your equity is less than 25%, calling is a mathematical leak that burns money.
lessons.proTip: Memorize the common bet sizes: Facing a half-pot bet = 25% required equity; facing a pot-sized bet = 33% required equity; facing a 2x pot overbet = 40% required equity.
lessons.commonMistake: Calling bets based on 'intuition' or 'a feeling' instead of calculating whether pot odds justify the price.
lessons.goldenRule: If your winning equity exceeds the required pot odds percentage, calling is mathematically mandatory.

decisionChallenge.question: The pot is $80. Villain bets $40. How much equity do you need to justify calling?
decisionChallenge.explanation: Cost to call = $40. Total pot after calling = $80 + $40 + $40 = $160. $40 / $160 = 25% required equity.

lessons.title: Counting Outs & The Rule of 2 and 4
lessons.coreConcept: An 'out' is any card in the deck that improves your hand to the winner. Multiply outs by 4 on the flop or by 2 on the turn.
lessons.content:
To compare your chances against Pot Odds, you must convert your drawing cards into an Equity Percentage.

**Step 1: Count Your Outs**
- Four to a Flush: There are 13 cards of each suit. You hold 2, board has 2. 13 - 4 = **9 outs**.
- Open-Ended Straight Draw (e.g., holding 8-9 on 6-7-K board): Any 5 or 10 makes a straight. 4 fives + 4 tens = **8 outs**.
- Gutshot Straight Draw (e.g., holding 8-9 on 6-10-K board): Only a 7 makes a straight = **4 outs**.
- Overcards (e.g., holding A-K on a 2-5-8 board): 3 remaining Aces + 3 remaining Kings = **6 outs**.

**Step 2: Apply the Rule of 2 and 4**
- **On the Flop (2 cards to come):** Multiply outs by **4**.
  * Flush draw: 9 outs * 4 ≈ **36% Equity**.
  * Open-ended straight draw: 8 outs * 4 ≈ **32% Equity**.
- **On the Turn (1 card to come):** Multiply outs by **2**.
  * Flush draw: 9 outs * 2 ≈ **18% Equity**.
  * Open-ended straight draw: 8 outs * 2 ≈ **16% Equity**.

Now compare: If facing a half-pot bet on the turn (requires 25%), calling with an open-ended straight draw (16%) is negative EV unless you have strong implied odds!
lessons.proTip: Discount dirty outs! If you are chasing a straight, but hitting your card also puts a flush on the board, subtract 1 or 2 outs because your straight may lose to a flush.
lessons.commonMistake: Chasing gutshot straight draws on the turn (4 outs * 2 = 8%) against large bets.
lessons.goldenRule: Count outs cleanly, multiply by 4 on the flop or 2 on the turn, and compare directly against pot odds.

lessons.title: Implied Odds vs. Reverse Implied Odds
lessons.coreConcept: Implied odds account for future chips you will win on later streets when you hit your hidden monster.
lessons.content:
Sometimes direct pot odds say you should fold, but calling is actually profitable because of **Implied Odds**.

Implied Odds factor in the future bets you expect to extract from your opponent on later streets if your draw hits. If an opponent is aggressive, deep-stacked, and loves their hand, you can call slightly unprofitable flop bets with suited connectors or pocket pairs because hitting your hidden set or straight will win their entire stack.

**Reverse Implied Odds (The Danger Zone):**
Reverse implied odds occur when hitting your card will still leave you second-best and cause you to lose a massive pot. For example, chasing a flush with 8♥ 4♥ when someone else holds A♥ K♥. Even if you hit your flush, you are drawing dead and will pay off a bigger flush.
lessons.proTip: High implied odds require: 1) Deep effective chip stacks, 2) A disguised hand (like a set or low straight), and 3) An opponent willing to pay off.
lessons.commonMistake: Calling huge bets with weak draws relying on implied odds against short-stacked opponents who have no chips left to pay you off on the river.
lessons.goldenRule: Implied odds make small investments profitable—ensure the potential payoff justifies the risk.

lessons.title: Quiz: Pot Odds & Equity Calculation
lessons.question: You are on the Turn with a 9-out flush draw. Villain bets $30 into a $60 pot. Using the Rule of 2 and 4, do you have enough equity to call?
options: No: You have ~18% equity and need 25%
Yes: You have ~36% equity and need 25%
Yes: You have ~50% equity and need 33%
No: You have ~8% equity and need 15%
lessons.correctAnswer: No: You have ~18% equity and need 25%

modules.title: Starting Hand Selection & Preflop Range Engineering
modules.description: Construct solid preflop opening ranges and balance VPIP and PFR.

lessons.title: Premium Hands vs. Speculative Hands
lessons.coreConcept: Premium hands make top pairs and high kickers; speculative hands make sets, straights, and flushes.
lessons.content:
In No-Limit Hold'em, starting hands fall into three strategic tiers:

**Tier 1: Premium Holdings (Top 5%)**
- Pocket Aces (AA), Kings (KK), Queens (QQ), Jacks (JJ), and Ace-King (AK).
- Strategy: Aggressively build the pot preflop with raises and 3-bets. Do not slowplay. You want to charge drawing hands and get maximum money in with preflop equity advantage.

**Tier 2: Speculative Hands (High Implied Odds)**
- Small pocket pairs (22 through 66) and suited connectors (89s, 9Ts, JTs).
- Strategy: In position, play these hands cheaply to flop a set (1 in 8 chance) or combination draw. When you hit a set with 44 on a K-9-4 board, your hand is disguised and opponents holding top pair will pay you off.

**Tier 3: Trap Hands (Negative Expected Value)**
- Offsuit broadways like K-10o, Q-Jo, A-8o, K-9o.
- Strategy: These look pretty but cause major reverse implied odds. When you hit top pair with a weak kicker, you win a small pot or lose a huge one.
lessons.proTip: Never limp speculative hands. If the pot is unopened, enter with a raise or fold. Raising gives you two ways to win: hitting your hand or winning the pot immediately preflop.
lessons.commonMistake: Cold-calling raises with offsuit Aces like A-7 offsuit, flopping an Ace, and losing three streets of bets to A-K.
lessons.goldenRule: Play premium hands for direct value; play speculative hands in position for implied odds.

lessons.title: VPIP & PFR: The Sacred Aggression Ratio
lessons.coreConcept: VPIP measures voluntary pot entry; PFR measures preflop raising. The narrower the gap, the stronger the player.
lessons.content:
In online poker analytics, two numbers define a player's fundamental skill level:

**VPIP (Voluntarily Put in Pot %):**
- The percentage of hands you voluntarily choose to play (calling or raising).
- A solid 6-max player maintains a VPIP between **22% and 26%**.
- If your VPIP is 40%+, you are playing loose and bleeding money.
- If your VPIP is 12%, you are playing too tight ('nit') and opponents will fold whenever you bet.

**PFR (Preflop Raise %):**
- The percentage of hands where you enter the pot with a raise.
- Solid players maintain a PFR between **18% and 22%**.

**The Golden Ratio (VPIP/PFR Gap):**
- If your VPIP is 24% and your PFR is 20%, you are a strong, aggressive player.
- If your VPIP is 38% and your PFR is 8%, you are a passive calling station ('fish'). You call frequently, rarely take initiative, and can be relentlessly bluffed.
lessons.proTip: Keep your VPIP/PFR gap under 5%. If a hand is good enough to call with preflop, it is almost always good enough to raise.
lessons.commonMistake: Limping preflop to 'see a cheap flop', allowing the big blind to see free flops with random cards that can outdraw you.
lessons.goldenRule: Close the gap between VPIP and PFR: entering pots with aggression commands respect and prints equity.

modules.title: Bet Sizing & Strategic Bluffing
modules.description: Learn the mechanics of value extraction, semi-bluffs, and geometric bet sizing.

lessons.title: The Art of Value Sizing
lessons.coreConcept: Target the exact hands your opponent can call with, and price your bet to extract maximum value.
lessons.content:
A **Value Bet** is placed when you believe you have the best hand and want a worse hand to call.

The key to elite value betting is sizing:
- If you bet too small ($10 into a $100 pot), your opponent calls easily, but you leave massive amounts of money on the table.
- If you bet too large ($100 into a $100 pot), your opponent folds everything except hands that beat you.

To pick the perfect size, ask yourself:
*What is the weakest hand in my opponent's range that will call me?*
- Against loose calling stations: Bet larger (66% to 80% pot) with your strong hands because they hate folding pairs.
- Against tight, disciplined opponents: Bet smaller (33% to 50% pot) to induce calls from third pair or weak bluff-catchers.
lessons.proTip: Geometric Bet Sizing: If you plan to bet all three streets, size your bets proportionally on Flop, Turn, and River so your stack moves into the pot smoothly without needing an awkward 3x pot river jam.
lessons.commonMistake: Checking the river with top pair out of fear, missing out on a clear street of value against weaker pairs.
lessons.goldenRule: Size your value bets to the maximum price your opponent's second-best hands are willing to pay.

lessons.title: Semi-Bluffing: The Dual-Path Strategy
lessons.coreConcept: A semi-bluff gives you two independent ways to win: fold equity right now, or hitting the winning card on the next street.
lessons.content:
A **Pure Bluff** has zero chance of improving if called. A **Semi-Bluff** is a bet made with a drawing hand (like a flush draw or open-ended straight draw) that is currently not the best hand, but has high potential to become the best hand.

Why Semi-Bluffing is the engine of modern aggression:
1. **Fold Equity**: The opponent folds, and you win the pot immediately with no showdown.
2. **Showdown Equity**: If the opponent calls, you still have outs to hit a monster on the turn or river.
3. **Deception**: When you hit your draw on the turn after betting the flop, your hand is disguised, and you win a huge pot.

Ideal Semi-Bluffing Hands: Combo draws (flush draw + gutshot = 12 outs), flush draws with an overcard, open-ended straight draws with backdoors.
lessons.proTip: Check-raising the flop as a semi-bluff with a combo draw is one of the highest-EV plays in poker. You put tremendous pressure on the preflop raiser.
lessons.commonMistake: Firing pure bluffs with zero outs on coordinated boards against calling stations.
lessons.goldenRule: Semi-bluff with equity: give yourself two ways to win every pot you contest.

modules.title: Bankroll Management & Tilt Control
modules.description: Essential financial and psychological armor required to survive poker variance.

lessons.title: The 30-to-100 Buy-in Rule
lessons.coreConcept: Variance is mathematical reality. Without proper bankroll depth, even a winning player will go broke.
lessons.content:
Even the best poker players in the world experience losing streaks that last weeks or months. This is called **Variance**.

To survive natural downswings, you must treat your bankroll as business capital separate from your living expenses:

**Cash Game Requirements:**
- Maintain a minimum of **30 to 40 Buy-Ins** for your chosen stake.
- If you play $1/$2 with a $200 max buy-in, your bankroll should be at least **$6,000 to $8,000**.
- If your bankroll drops below 25 buy-ins, move down in stakes immediately to rebuild.

**Tournament (MTT) Requirements:**
- Tournaments have significantly higher variance than cash games.
- Maintain at least **100 Buy-Ins** for the average tournament buy-in level.

Moving up in stakes should only occur when you have crushed your current stake over a large sample (20,000+ hands) and have 40+ buy-ins for the next level.
lessons.proTip: Never play with money you cannot afford to lose. The psychological fear of losing 'rent money' causes scared, passive play that destroys your edge.
lessons.commonMistake: Jumping up in stakes after a winning weekend, getting stacked, and losing the entire bankroll.
lessons.goldenRule: Bankroll management guarantees survival: play within your bankroll to let math work in your favor.

lessons.title: Emotional Armor & The Stop-Loss Protocol
lessons.coreConcept: Recognizing cognitive distortion and enforcing session stop-loss limits protects your bankroll from destruction.
lessons.content:
Tilt takes many forms:
1. **Running-Bad Tilt**: Feeling victimized by luck after multiple bad beats.
2. **Injustice Tilt**: Believing the poker gods are out to get you.
3. **Entitlement Tilt**: Believing you 'deserve' to win a pot because you are the better player.
4. **Revenge Tilt**: Singling out a specific player who stacked you and aggressively targeting them out of spite.

**The Professional Stop-Loss Protocol:**
- Set a rigid session stop-loss of **3 Buy-Ins**.
- If you lose 3 buy-ins in a single session, close the tables immediately, regardless of how good the game looks.
- Take a 24-hour break, review hand histories when calm, and return with a clear mind.
lessons.proTip: When you feel your heart rate accelerating or feel the urge to shove all-in with any two cards to 'get even', you are in red-zone tilt. Step away from the computer immediately.
lessons.commonMistake: Chasing losses by depositing more money immediately after a bad beat.
lessons.goldenRule: Your discipline when losing defines your winrate far more than your play when winning.

modules.title: The Preflop Masterclass
modules.description: Construct rock-solid preflop opening and defense ranges from every position.

lessons.title: Raise First In (RFI) by Position
lessons.coreConcept: Your opening range should expand smoothly as you move from Under the Gun to the Button.
lessons.content:
RFI ('Raise First In') occurs when everyone folds to you and you are the first player to enter the pot with a raise.

Professional 6-Max RFI Frequencies by Position:
- **UTG (Under the Gun): ~14% to 16%** (Pairs 66+, ATo+, A2s+, broadways)
- **MP (Middle Position / Hijack): ~18% to 22%** (Pairs 44+, suited connectors 78s+)
- **CO (Cutoff): ~26% to 30%** (Pairs 22+, suited gappers 86s+, suited broadways)
- **BTN (Button): ~42% to 48%** (Any pair, almost any suited card, strong offsuits)
- **SB (Small Blind): ~36% to 42%** (Steal attempt against the Big Blind)

Notice the progression: As fewer players remain behind you, you can profitably raise more than triple the number of hands on the Button compared to Under the Gun.
lessons.proTip: Use a standard raise size of 2.5x the big blind from late position, and 2.5x to 3x from early position.
lessons.commonMistake: Opening the exact same hands from UTG as you do on the Button.
lessons.goldenRule: Expand your opening range progressively as position improves toward the button.

lessons.title: The 3-Bet: Taking Preflop Control
lessons.coreConcept: A 3-bet is a re-raise over an initial open. It asserts range dominance and isolates weaker opponents.
lessons.content:
Terminology:
- Blinds = 1st bet.
- Initial Open = 2nd bet.
- Re-Raise = **3-Bet**.

A well-constructed 3-betting range is not just Aces and Kings. Modern strategy uses a **Linear or Polarized 3-Bet Range**:

**Value 3-Bets:** Hands that are thrilled to get called or 4-bet (AA, KK, QQ, AKs, AKo).
**Bluff / Semi-Bluff 3-Bets:** Hands with great playability and blockers that don't want to flat-call (A5s, A4s, KJs, QTs, 87s).

Why 3-Betting A-5 Suited is brilliant:
1. Card Removal: You hold an Ace, cutting the probability that your opponent holds Pocket Aces in half.
2. Playability: If called, you can flop the nut flush, a wheel straight (A-2-3-4-5), or top pair with backdoor equity.
lessons.proTip: 3-Bet larger out of position! If an opponent opens to $6, 3-bet to $18 in position (3x), but 3-bet to $24 out of position (4x) to compensate for acting first postflop.
lessons.commonMistake: Only 3-betting Pocket Aces and Kings, making your strategy completely transparent to observant opponents.
lessons.goldenRule: Mix value and playable blockers into your 3-betting range to keep opponents guessing.

tracks.volumeTitle: Volume 3: Modern GTO & Advanced Strategic Concepts
tracks.title: Advanced: Game Theory Optimal (GTO) & Exploitation
tracks.description: Unlock modern solver concepts: Minimum Defense Frequency, Range Advantage, Blockers, and Tournament ICM.

modules.title: The Solver Revolution & GTO Foundations
modules.description: Understand Nash Equilibrium and mathematically unexploitable poker play.

lessons.title: What is Game Theory Optimal (GTO)?
lessons.coreConcept: GTO is a defensive mathematical equilibrium. If you play GTO, no opponent can exploit you in the long run.
lessons.content:
Game Theory Optimal (GTO) is derived from John Nash's Nobel Prize-winning concept of Nash Equilibrium.

In poker, a GTO strategy is an unexploitable strategy. It means your ranges, bet sizes, checking frequencies, and bluffing percentages are so mathematically balanced that even if your opponent knew your exact strategy chart in advance, they could not profit against you.

GTO serves as your home base. You do not play GTO to crush bad players; you play GTO to understand the mathematical baseline of correct poker. Once you know what optimal play looks like, you can spot where opponents deviate and exploit them.
lessons.proTip: Do not treat GTO as a rigid script. GTO is a diagnostic framework: learn what equilibrium requires so you know when to deviate profitably.
lessons.commonMistake: Trying to play pure GTO against weak recreational players who call everything—against them, pure exploitative value betting is far more profitable.
lessons.goldenRule: Master GTO as your baseline; deviate with exploitative plays to punish amateur mistakes.

lessons.title: Minimum Defense Frequency (MDF)
lessons.coreConcept: MDF is the minimum percentage of your range you must defend with to prevent opponent bluffs from auto-profiting.
lessons.content:
When an opponent bets, how often must you call or raise to keep them honest?

**The MDF Formula:**
**MDF = Pot Size / (Pot Size + Bet Size)**

Example:
- Pot is $100. Villain bets $50.
- MDF = $100 / ($100 + $50) = $100 / $150 = **66.7%**.
- This means you must continue (call or raise) with at least 66.7% of the hands in your range. If you fold more than 33.3%, villain can blindly bluff with any two random cards and print automatic profit.

Example Facing an Overbet:
- Pot is $100. Villain bets $150 (overbet).
- MDF = $100 / ($100 + $150) = $100 / $250 = **40%**.
- Against large overbets, you are mathematically permitted to fold 60% of your range!
lessons.proTip: Use MDF as a defense benchmark on the river. If folding would mean folding your top 40% of hands, you must make the call.
lessons.commonMistake: Over-folding to small 1/3 pot c-bets where the required defense frequency is over 75%.
lessons.goldenRule: MDF guards your bankroll: defend often enough that opponents cannot profitably bluff with air.

modules.title: Range Advantage & C-Bet Strategy
modules.description: Analyze board textures through the lens of range advantage and nut advantage.

lessons.title: Range Advantage vs. Nut Advantage
lessons.coreConcept: Range advantage dictates who can bet frequently; nut advantage dictates who can bet huge.
lessons.content:
Not all advantages on the flop are created equal:

**Range Advantage (Overall Equity):**
- Who has the higher average equity across their entire range of cards?
- If you raised preflop from UTG and the Big Blind called, on an **A-K-7 rainbow flop**, you hold a massive range advantage. You hold all the AA, KK, AK, and AQ, while the Big Blind rarely has these hands.
- Strategy with Range Advantage: Bet small (25% to 33% pot) with a very high frequency (70%+ of your range).

**Nut Advantage (The Top Tier Hands):**
- Who holds the super-monsters (Sets, Two Pairs, Straights)?
- On an **8♠ 7♠ 6♦ flop**, the Big Blind holds nut advantage because their defending range contains 87s, 76s, 65s, 88, 77, 66, and 9T offsuit—hands UTG folded preflop.
- Strategy with Nut Advantage: Check-raise and bet large (75%+ pot) to pressure overpairs.
lessons.proTip: Never blindly c-bet flops that heavily favor the caller's range (like 6-7-8 wet boards). Check back to protect your range.
lessons.commonMistake: C-betting 100% of flops as preflop raiser regardless of whether the board favors you or the caller.
lessons.goldenRule: Bet small and often with range advantage; bet large and aggressive with nut advantage.

lessons.title: Continuation Bet (C-Bet) Frequencies
lessons.coreConcept: Flop texture determines whether modern solvers choose a high-frequency small bet or a polar check.
lessons.content:
A **Continuation Bet (C-Bet)** is a flop bet placed by the preflop aggressor.

Modern C-Betting Strategy by Texture:
1. **High, Dry Boards (e.g., A♦ 8♠ 2♣, K♠ 7♦ 3♣):**
   - Range Bet: Bet **33% pot with 80% to 100% of your range**.
   - Reason: You hold massive range advantage. Small bets force opponents to fold missed cards while offering you a cheap price to win the pot.
2. **Dynamic, Coordinated Boards (e.g., Q♥ J♥ 8♣, 9♦ 8♦ 6♠):**
   - Polarized Strategy: Bet **66% to 75% pot with 40% of your range**, and check the remaining 60%.
   - Reason: The caller's range hits these boards hard. You must bet strong hands for protection and check marginal hands to keep the pot small.
lessons.proTip: Check back top pair with weak kicker on wet boards to control the pot size and catch river bluffs.
lessons.commonMistake: Betting 75% pot on an Ace-high dry board when a 25% bet accomplishes the exact same result for one-third the risk.
lessons.goldenRule: Size down on dry boards with range edge; size up on wet boards to deny opponent equity.

modules.title: Advanced Range Construction & Blockers
modules.description: Construct polarized and merged ranges, and harness card removal in bluff-catching.

lessons.title: Polarized vs. Condensed / Merged Ranges
lessons.coreConcept: Polarized ranges bet nuts and bluffs; merged ranges bet strong to medium value hands.
lessons.content:
Understanding range polarization is the dividing line between advanced players and intermediate players:

**A Polarized Range:**
- Consists of two extremes: **The Absolute Nuts** + **Pure Air Bluffs**.
- There are no medium-strength hands in a polarized bet.
- Optimal Sizing: Large bets (75% to 150% pot) or overbets.
- Example: On the river, you bet 1.5x pot holding either a Nut Flush or a completely busted straight draw.

**A Condensed / Merged Range:**
- Consists primarily of **Medium to Strong hands** (Top Pair good kicker, second pair, two pair).
- There are few pure bluffs and few absolute nuts.
- Optimal Sizing: Small to medium bets (33% to 50% pot).
- Purpose: Thin value betting and blocking bets to reach a cheap showdown.
lessons.proTip: When you bet large, your range must be polarized. If you bet 125% pot with a medium hand, you isolate yourself against hands that beat you.
lessons.commonMistake: Overbetting the river with middle pair, turning a showdown-value hand into a bluff.
lessons.goldenRule: Polarize large bets with nuts and bluffs; condense small bets around value and pot control.

lessons.title: Blockers & Card Removal in Bluff-Catching
lessons.coreConcept: Holding key cards reduces the mathematical probability that your opponent holds a monster.
lessons.content:
A **Blocker** (Card Removal effect) occurs when a card in your private hand makes it statistically less likely for your opponent to hold specific combinations.

Classic Examples of Blockers in Action:
1. **The Ace of the Flush Suit (The Nut Blocker):**
   - Board has 3 hearts: K♥ 8♥ 2♥.
   - You hold **A♥ 4♠**.
   - Even though you do not have a flush yet, you hold the A♥. It is mathematically IMPOSSIBLE for your opponent to have the Nut Flush! You can use this blocker to fire a devastating bluff.
2. **Bluff-Catching on the River:**
   - The river brings a potential straight (e.g., board has 7-8-9-J).
   - You hold a Pair of Tens. Holding a Ten blocks your opponent from having the Q-10 or 10-6 straight. Your Ten blocker makes it vastly safer to call a river bet.
lessons.proTip: When deciding which missed draws to turn into river bluffs, prioritize hands with good blockers (blocking villain's calling hands) and unblockers (unblocking villain's folding hands).
lessons.commonMistake: Bluff-catching while holding the exact cards your opponent would have missed a draw with.
lessons.goldenRule: Use blockers to deduce what opponents cannot hold: card removal unlocks razor-thin calls and bluffs.

modules.title: Exploitative Play & Player Archetypes
modules.description: Deviate from GTO to systematically destroy recreational player leaks.

lessons.title: GTO vs. Exploitative Counter-Strategies
lessons.coreConcept: GTO is defensive equilibrium; Exploitative play maximizes profit by directly attacking opponent leaks.
lessons.content:
While GTO guarantees you cannot lose, **Exploitative Play** maximizes your dollar-per-hour winrate by identifying what your opponent does wrong and counter-punching:

**Archetype 1: The Calling Station (Passive Fish)**
- Leak: Calls far too often with weak pairs; never folds draws; rarely raises without the nuts.
- Counter-Exploit: **NEVER bluff them**. Expand your value-betting range dramatically. Bet third pair for value and size up your monsters to 80%+ pot.

**Archetype 2: The 'Nit' (Rock / Ultra-Tight)**
- Leak: Plays only premium cards; folds everything else; raises only with monsters.
- Counter-Exploit: **Steal their blinds relentlessly**. Fold instantly whenever they raise you, even if you hold Top Pair Top Kicker—a Nit's raise is always two pair or better.

**Archetype 3: The Aggressive Maniac**
- Leak: Over-bluffs every street; cannot stand checking; bets every river.
- Counter-Exploit: **Induce bluffs**. Check your strong hands to let them hang themselves with air.
lessons.proTip: When an opponent shows a clear extreme leak, abandon GTO balance immediately. Maximum exploitation generates 3x to 5x higher winrates in low-to-mid stakes games.
lessons.commonMistake: Trying to run complex triple-barrel bluffs against calling stations who 'just want to see your cards'.
lessons.goldenRule: Identify the leak and counter-attack: value-bet the stations, bluff the nits, and trap the maniacs.

tracks.description: Step-by-step tactical breakdowns of iconic high-level poker plays used by tournament champions and high-stakes pros.

modules.title: Preflop Combat Plays
modules.description: Aggressive preflop weapons to capture dead money and dominate position.

lessons.title: Play #1: The Squeeze Play
lessons.coreConcept: Punish an initial raiser and weak callers by executing a massive 3-bet to scoop dead money.
lessons.content:
The **Squeeze Play** is one of the most profitable preflop plays in poker.

**The Setup:**
1. A player in middle position opens with a standard raise.
2. One or two loose players flat-call behind them.
3. You are in the Cutoff, Button, or Big Blind with a playable holding.

**The Execution:**
- Because the initial raiser faced callers, their range is wide. Because the callers flat-called instead of 3-betting, their ranges are capped and weak.
- There is now a massive amount of 'dead money' sitting in the pot.
- You fire a large **Squeeze 3-Bet** (usually 4.5x to 5.5x the original open).

**The Outcome:**
- The initial raiser is trapped between you and the callers, forcing them to fold marginal hands.
- The callers, having already demonstrated weakness, fold. You rake in a massive pot without even having to see a flop!
lessons.proTip: Ideal squeeze hands: Suited Aces (A5s, A4s) because they hold Ace card removal, or big broadways (A-Q, K-Q).
lessons.commonMistake: Squeezing too small (e.g. 3x open), offering callers irresistible pot odds to call and draw against you multi-way.
lessons.goldenRule: Size your squeeze aggressively to punish capped flat-callers and claim dead money.

lessons.title: Play #2: The Button Blind Steal & Re-Steal
lessons.coreConcept: Systematically extract profit from tight blinds, and counter late-position steals with 3-bet re-steals.
lessons.content:
In modern poker, the blinds are where winrates are won or lost.

**The Steal (From Button or Cutoff):**
- When action folds to you on the Button, open-raise 45% to 50% of your starting cards to 2.2x to 2.5x the big blind.
- If the Small Blind and Big Blind fold more than 62% of the time combined, your raise prints instant profit before postflop play even begins.

**The Re-Steal (From Small Blind or Big Blind):**
- When an active Button attempts to steal your blind, do not passively flat-call.
- Fire a **3-Bet Re-Steal** (to 9x to 10x the big blind) with suited broadways, suited connectors, or playable Aces.
- You turn the tables on the steal attempt and force the button to fold their bottom 70% of cards.
lessons.proTip: Target tight players in the blinds. If the big blind has a VPIP under 15%, steal with almost any two cards.
lessons.commonMistake: Flat-calling from the Small Blind against a button raise, entering the flop out of position with a multi-way trap.
lessons.goldenRule: Steal relentlessly from the button; punish habitual stealers with aggressive 3-bet re-steals.

modules.title: Postflop Tactical Weapons
modules.description: Master check-raises, delayed c-bets, and multi-street pressure.

lessons.title: Play #3: The Check-Raise Semi-Bluff
lessons.coreConcept: Overcome positional disadvantage by check-raising the flop with combination draws.
lessons.content:
Being out of position is a handicap—unless you know how to wield the **Check-Raise**.

**The Scenario:**
- You defend the Big Blind with **7♠ 8♠** against a Cutoff open.
- Flop comes: **6♠ 9♦ 2♠** (Monster Combo Draw: Open-Ended Straight Draw + Flush Draw = 15 outs!).

**The Execution:**
1. You check to the preflop raiser.
2. Villain fires a standard 1/3 pot c-bet ($20 into $60).
3. Instead of passively calling, you **Check-Raise to $70** (3.5x their bet).

**Why This Play Is Brutal:**
- Villain must fold all their missed broadways, overcards, and weak pairs.
- If Villain calls, you have 15 outs (54% equity) to make a straight or flush by the river. You are actually the statistical favorite to win the hand!
lessons.proTip: Balance your check-raise semi-bluffs with nut value check-raises (like flopped Sets with 6-6 or 2-2) so opponents can never tell whether you hold quads or a combo draw.
lessons.commonMistake: Check-calling flop draws passively and folding the turn when you miss, throwing away chips with zero fold equity.
lessons.goldenRule: Seize the offensive from out of position: check-raise combo draws to maximize fold and showdown equity.

lessons.title: Play #4: The Delayed Continuation Bet
lessons.coreConcept: Checking the flop in position to attack the turn with a delayed continuation bet.
lessons.content:
Most amateurs believe that if you raise preflop, you must bet the flop. Enter the **Delayed C-Bet**.

**How It Works:**
1. You raise preflop on the Button and the Big Blind calls.
2. On the flop, the Big Blind checks. Instead of betting, you **Check Back**.
3. On the turn, the Big Blind checks to you a second time.
4. You now fire a **Delayed C-Bet** (50% to 66% pot).

**Why This Play Prints Money:**
- When the Big Blind checks the turn a second time, they are screaming that they have a weak, marginal hand.
- Your flop check under-represented your strength, inducing bluffs or allowing you to steal the pot cheaply on the turn.
- It provides perfect pot control with medium hands like Second Pair Top Kicker.
lessons.proTip: Delayed c-betting works best on draw-heavy flops that turn into brick turn cards.
lessons.commonMistake: C-betting 100% of flops and then giving up on the turn when called.
lessons.goldenRule: Use the delayed c-bet to control pot sizes and exploit opponents who check twice in weakness.

modules.title: River Warfare & Climax Plays
modules.description: Execute triple-barrel bluffs and extract razor-thin river value.

lessons.title: Play #5: The Triple Barrel Bluff
lessons.coreConcept: Telling a consistent, terrifying story across all three streets to fold out top pairs on the river.
lessons.content:
The **Triple Barrel Bluff** (betting Flop, Turn, and River as a bluff) is the highest-level psychological play in poker.

**When to Execute a Triple Barrel:**
1. **Board Runout:** The turn and river bring scare cards (like an Ace, King, or four-to-a-flush) that heavily favor YOUR preflop range and crush your opponent's capped calling range.
2. **Opponent Profile:** Target 'Fit-or-Fold' or tight players who hate risking tournament life or full stacks with one pair.
3. **Blockers:** You hold key blockers to the winning hands (e.g., holding the A♣ on a 4-club board).

When you fire 75% pot on the river after betting flop and turn, your bet screams: 'I have the nuts, and you must call for your tournament life with top pair.' Discipline wins out, and opponents fold winning hands.
lessons.proTip: Never triple-barrel into calling stations who brag about calling down with bottom pair. Only bluff players with the mental discipline to fold.
lessons.commonMistake: Triple barreling on river runouts that improve your opponent's calling range (like a card that pairs the board).
lessons.goldenRule: A credible triple barrel requires scare card runouts and an opponent capable of laying down top pair.

lessons.title: Play #6: The Thin Value River Bet
lessons.coreConcept: Extracting the final 10 to 15 big blinds on the river with second-best pairs against recreational callers.
lessons.content:
Amateurs only bet the river with the nuts. High-stakes crushers make their fortune with **Thin Value Bets**.

A Thin Value Bet is a bet made with a marginal hand (like Second Pair Top Kicker, or weak Top Pair) where you anticipate being called by worse hands **just over 50% of the time**.

**How to Price a Thin Value Bet:**
- When your hand is marginal, a large 75% pot bet will only be called by better hands.
- But a small **20% to 33% pot bet** gives your opponent irresistible 5:1 or 6:1 pot odds. They feel priced in to call with third pair, ace-high, or pocket pairs below the board.
- Over 1,000 hands, extracting 15 extra big blinds from thin value adds 5 to 8 BB/100 to your overall winrate!
lessons.proTip: If raised on a thin value bet, fold immediately! You bet for thin value, not to contest a raise. An opponent raising a river bet almost always holds the nuts.
lessons.commonMistake: Checking back the river in fear of being raised, forfeiting free chips that recreational players would happily pay.
lessons.goldenRule: Size thin value bets small to entice calls from worse hands, and fold without hesitation if raised.
